characterList.name: Lecturer

content_metadata.description: A lecture detailing the concepts of Gibbs free energy and chemical potential in thermodynamics. The lecturer explains the equations and the underlying principles involving Gibbs free energy and how it relates to chemical potential.

qAndA.question: What is the equation for Gibbs free energy?

qAndA.answer: The Gibbs free energy per particle when temperature and pressure are fixed.
qAndA.question: What does the chemical potential represent?

qAndA.answer: Because it does not change when the size of the system (number of particles) increases while other intensive properties like temperature and pressure are held fixed.
qAndA.question: Why is the chemical potential considered an intensive property?

qAndA.answer: The chemical potential is likely to change, as volume is an extensive property that changes with the number of particles.
qAndA.question: What happens to the chemical potential if both volume and number of particles are changed?

qAndA.answer: Because in that case, you are holding an extensive property (volume) fixed, while changing another extensive property (number of particles). This violates the condition for the chemical potential to remain constant.
qAndA.question: Why can't you use the partial derivative of Helmholtz free energy with respect to the number of particles to calculate the chemical potential if you hold temperature and volume fixed?

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer introduces himself and the topic of the video.
The lecturer begins explaining the Gibbs free energy equation.
The lecturer explains the concept of constant pressure and temperature in relation to Gibbs free energy.
The lecturer writes the equation for the infinitesimal change in Gibbs free energy.
The lecturer explains the concept of chemical potential.
The lecturer explains the relationship between the partial derivative of Gibbs free energy with respect to the number of particles and the chemical potential.
The lecturer explains the concepts of extensive and intensive properties.
The lecturer revisits the Gibbs free energy equation and explains its implications for the chemical potential.
The lecturer emphasizes that the chemical potential represents the Gibbs free energy per particle.
The lecturer uses a similar partial derivative to illustrate a contrast and further explain the concept of chemical potential.
The lecturer emphasizes that the chemical potential can change when the number of particles increases if other variables like volume are not held constant.
The lecturer reiterates that the chemical potential is the Gibbs free energy per particle when temperature and pressure are held fixed.

youtube_description:
In this video I continue with my series of tutorial videos on Thermal Physics and Thermodynamics.  It's pitched at undergraduate level and while it is mainly aimed at physics majors, it should be useful to anybody taking a first course in thermodynamics such as engineers etc..

The course covers topics such as the Ideal Gas Law, Entropy, Enthalpy, Gibbs' and Helmholtz' Free Energy, Heat Capacity, Einstein Solids, Taylor and MacLaurin Series / Expansions, phase transformations, thermodynamics identities, the Clausius Clapeyron Relation, Joule Thompson Throttling, Adiabatic Cooling, the paramagnet and of course the all important Laws of Thermodynamics

Thank you for watching and I hope that this matches your requirements. Please feel free to provide feedback via comments and share with your friends.

See my website for more: www.universityphysicstutorials.com
Follow me on Twitter @adambeatty503
Follow me on Facebook UniversityPhysicsTutorials
